name: Jaw surgery (orthognathic)

lead: Orthognathic surgery repositions the upper jaw, lower jaw, chin or all three. In looksmaxxing communities it is treated as the major structural option for a recessed jaw, facial balance, profile and a straighter bite and smile; medically it is used for underbites, overbites, open bites, asymmetry, jaw-joint problems and sleep apnoea.

Surgeons cut the jawbones from inside the mouth, move them to a planned position and fix them with titanium plates and screws, usually after orthodontic preparation. Procedures include Le Fort I for the upper jaw, sagittal split for the lower jaw and genioplasty for the chin, sometimes combined as two-jaw (bimaxillary) surgery. Virtual 3D planning and custom splints are increasingly used. Medical literature documents functional outcomes well and is more limited on purely cosmetic goals.

paras: People typically go through orthodontics first, often braces, then surgery planned with a surgeon and orthodontist, followed by recovery over weeks to months. Forum discussion centers on surgeon choice, insurance, braces timing and recovery.

Reviews describe bleeding, swelling, infection, nerve numbness, jaw-joint effects, relapse and hardware problems, with recovery lasting weeks to months. A systematic review estimated body dysmorphic disorder is more common among orthognathic surgery patients than in the general community.

web.title: Men are going to extremes to get manlier jaws (Newser)

angle.text: Orthognathic surgery cuts and repositions the upper jaw, lower jaw and chin, realigning the bite and midface for better facial balance and profile. The change in jaw position is itself the visible result, though reports note functional gains and cosmetic outcomes do not always match.

lead: Orthognathic surgery, also called corrective jaw surgery, reshapes and repositions the upper jaw (maxilla), lower jaw (mandible) and chin. It is a recognised branch of oral and maxillofacial surgery used to treat bite discrepancies, growth-related jaw problems, jaw-joint disorders and airway obstruction, and it is also used to improve facial balance and symmetry.[1][2] The operation is performed mostly through incisions inside the mouth, so that no facial scars result: bone is cut, moved to a planned position and fixed with small titanium plates and screws.[1][3]

For appearance, the appeal is that it moves the skeleton that the soft tissues drape over. A recessed upper jaw, a weak or set-back lower jaw, a long lower face, a gummy smile, an underbite or a crooked chin can each be changed by moving bone, and surgeons plan the move against profile and frontal facial analysis as well as the bite.[1][4][5] Two-jaw (bimaxillary or 'bimax') operations combine a Le Fort I osteotomy of the upper jaw with a bilateral sagittal split osteotomy of the lower jaw, often with a chin genioplasty added.[1][3][6] The procedure is nearly always coordinated with orthodontics, traditionally with braces before and after surgery.[1]

The research literature is large and mostly concerned with function, planning accuracy, stability and complications. Reviews describe expanding indications over the past two decades, including airway obstruction, along with computer-assisted planning, patient-specific fixation and changes in how orthodontics and surgery are sequenced.[7] Surgeons and researchers also study aesthetic outcomes, and a systematic review comparing orthodontic camouflage with surgical-orthodontic treatment for skeletal class II patients reported that the surgical route produced larger changes in several skeletal and soft-tissue profile measures.[8]

In looksmaxxing communities jaw surgery is regarded as one of the most consequential 'hardmaxx' procedures, discussed alongside facial implants, rhinoplasty and orthodontics, with long threads on surgeon selection, travelling abroad, braces, recovery and complications.[9][10][11] Surgeons and news outlets have also commented on the growing number of men seeking it for a more defined jawline, and some clinicians have cautioned about its permanence.[12][13]

paras: The Le Fort I osteotomy frees the upper jaw so that it can be moved forward, back, up, down or tilted. It is described in dedicated reviews that cover indications, contraindications, preoperative assessment, technique and complications, and it is the main maxillary operation used in two-jaw surgery.[4][14] It is used for vertical maxillary excess ('long face'), a deficient or retruded maxilla and some bite problems.[1][4]

The bilateral sagittal split osteotomy (BSSO) splits each side of the lower jaw lengthwise so that the tooth-bearing segment can be slid forward or back, with the inferior alveolar nerve protected during the split. The bone is then fixed with plates and screws.[1] Older descriptions involved wiring the jaws shut for weeks; modern fixation generally avoids long periods of immobilisation.[1][2]

Genioplasty repositions the chin by cutting and sliding a segment of the chin bone, or alternatively by placing an implant; it may be done alone or alongside jaw surgery. Contemporary reviews describe it as an essential component when chin position affects lower-face aesthetics and cover techniques, stability, fixation and complications.[1][3] Surgically assisted palatal expansion widens a narrow upper jaw, and forum members sometimes discuss it alongside, or as an alternative to, orthodontic expanders such as MARPE.[1]

Asymmetry cases are described as challenging because each face is individual; 3D diagnosis and virtual planning have been described as increasingly helpful in producing symmetry.[5] Orthognathic surgery is also used for cleft lip and palate patients whose upper jaw is three-dimensionally deficient, where reviews describe extra challenges from earlier scarring and dental differences.[15]

Wikipedia dates one of the earliest published orthognathic cases to 1849, by the American surgeon Simon P. Hullihen, and says that jaw osteotomies for malocclusion and prognathism developed in the 1940s.[1] Overviews attribute much of the modern era to the 1950s and 1960s, when the bilateral sagittal split and the modern form of the Le Fort I osteotomy were developed.[2]

Hugo Obwegeser, an Austrian surgeon born in 1920 who trained under Richard Trauner in Graz, is widely credited with popularising the sagittal split of the lower jaw and with developing the modern Le Fort I procedure, which fully mobilises the upper jaw. He introduced his techniques to North American surgeons at a 1966 meeting at Walter Reed and described simultaneous operation on both jaws around 1969-1970. He died in 2017.[6] Wikipedia notes that the term itself is credited to Harold Hargis.[1]

The 1970s brought rigid internal fixation with titanium plates, which reduced the need to wire the jaws shut and improved stability.[2] The hierarchy of stability for different surgical movements was updated in 2007 to include correction of asymmetry and chin repositioning, both reported as stable with rigid fixation.[16] In 2002 Raffaini described performing sagittal osteotomy under local anaesthesia with intravenous sedation to avoid prolonged hospital stays.[1]

From the 2000s onward, cone-beam CT, 3D virtual planning, computer-generated splints and cutting guides, and patient-specific implants have changed practice, and clinical trials continue to register studies of custom plates and guides.[7][17][18][19] Wikipedia lists newer variants including surgery-first approaches that delay braces until after the operation.[1]

A surgical team usually includes an oral and maxillofacial surgeon and an orthodontist, and sometimes a speech and language therapist; radiographs, photographs and 3D software are used to predict the result and to help patients understand the plan.[1] Wikipedia also notes that a psychological assessment is sometimes used to judge expectations.[1] Planning has to account for the airway, since moving the jaws can change its dimensions, and clinical trials have registered studies of upper-airway volume change after surgery.[1][20]

Presurgical orthodontics has traditionally taken up to a year to align the teeth over their jaws, though surgery-first approaches and clear aligners are described as newer options.[1] A randomised trial compared periodontal health and quality of life in post-surgical patients treated with clear aligners versus fixed appliances.[21]

Cephalometric analysis, the measurement of angles and distances on skull radiographs, underpins much planning; widely cited papers describe cephalometric methods for orthognathic patients and soft-tissue analysis aimed at good facial aesthetics.[22][23] A systematic review of 12 studies found virtual planning accurate to under 2 mm on average in the maxilla and mandible in three planes, a prospective multicentre study of 65 patients compared a computer-aided simulation protocol with actual outcomes,[17] and trials have compared maxilla-guided and mandible-guided approaches using patient-specific implants.[24]

Human research on orthognathic surgery covers planning accuracy, stability, complications, patient-reported outcomes and sleep apnoea. A hierarchy-of-stability update reported that stability differs among surgical movements, with correction of asymmetry and chin repositioning very stable under rigid fixation.[16] A review of 655 patients examined the incidence of complications and problems after orthognathic surgery.[25]

For sleep apnoea, a 2016 individual-patient meta-analysis examined criteria associated with outcomes of maxillomandibular advancement,[26] and Wikipedia cites a 1999 study of 50 patients reporting success rates of 90-100 percent for the operation.[1]

On aesthetics, a systematic review and meta-analysis of orthodontic camouflage versus surgical-orthodontic treatment in adult class II patients with a retrognathic mandible (nine studies, seven in the meta-analysis) found no statistically significant difference for several profile measures, but greater effectiveness of the surgical route for several skeletal angles and for the soft-tissue profile including the nose; the authors urged caution given the limited number of studies.[8]

Psychological outcomes have been examined too. A systematic review found a weighted prevalence of body dysmorphic disorder of 11.2 percent in orthognathic surgery settings, compared with 1.9 percent in the adult community, and noted that the condition is poorly identified in practice.[27] Other trials have compared post-surgical orthodontic methods and surgical guidance approaches,[21][24] and a 2024 clinical trial examined changes in taste sensation after orthognathic surgery.[28]

Wikipedia describes initial healing as taking about two to six weeks, with a further two to four months for full bone healing and remodelling, a liquid or soft diet for a period with some weight loss, and a return to work typically after two to six weeks.[1] Swelling and bruising peak in the first days and mostly resolve over a few weeks, though some swelling can last months.[1][2]

An AI-generated encyclopedia overview reports that most patients achieve stable occlusion with high satisfaction and quality-of-life improvement, and describes full bone healing as taking 6 to 12 months; the same overview notes that aesthetic concerns are considered mainly where function is also affected and that candidates are screened for body dysmorphic disorder. These statements come from an untrusted summary and should be read against the peer-reviewed literature.[2]

Wikipedia lists bleeding, swelling, infection, nausea and nerve-related numbness as the main risks, with infection reported in up to 7 percent of cases in general reports and numbness usually temporary, typically resolving within about three months, though occasionally permanent.[1] It also reports a study in which infection of jaw hardware was far more common when third molars were removed at the same operation, which led to the practice of not combining the two.[1] Some movements, such as maxillary impaction, are described as carrying higher complication risk.[1]

Longer-term issues described in reviews include relapse of jaw position, jaw-joint symptoms, hardware problems and occasional dissatisfaction, and a classic 655-patient review catalogued complications by type.[2][25] The body dysmorphic disorder finding is why surgeons describe expectation-setting and psychological screening as important.[1][27]

A forum member's long post summarising complications reported on forums and social media lists nerve damage, persistent numbness and altered sensation among the issues patients describe; another member who had a double-jaw operation for sleep apnoea reported good functional results but an unsatisfactory aesthetic outcome and later bone contouring.[11][10]

Forum threads describe jaw surgery as a major step for people with a recessed or underdeveloped jaw, discussing whether to have a bimaxillary or single-jaw operation, when to start orthodontics, how age affects eligibility and whether the result will look better than a jaw-jut test in photographs suggests.[9] Some posters are teenagers asking whether to wait until 18 and whether one maxillary technique is preferable to another.[29]

Threads also discuss price, recovery time, expectations of masculinisation and which surgeons offer the strongest aesthetic results. In one thread a poster considering a double-jaw operation with genioplasty in Poland sets 'maximum aesthetic improvement' rather than medical correction as the goal and asks for before-and-after photographs from several clinics.[30] Members compare surgeons known for functional versus aesthetic emphasis, discuss surgery abroad, and compare jaw surgery with implants and other procedures.[10][11][30]

News coverage of the trend includes a 2023 GQ feature, summarised by Newser, that profiled a Barcelona surgeon who said he performed around 200 orthofacial surgeries a year and reported a rise in international male patients, particularly from tech, with the pandemic and video calls making men focus on their jawlines.[12] The same coverage linked the trend to looksmaxxing forums.[12] In 2026 a UT Southwestern plastic surgeon wrote that influencers recommend major and permanent operations such as bimaxillary osteotomy and Le Fort I advancement for cosmetic reasons, while such bone surgery is typically recommended for congenital deformities or injury.[13]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org jaw surgery appears in threads on planning, braces, surgeon selection, recovery and complications, from first-time patients to people reporting revisions, and it is often described as a structural 'hardmaxx' option.[9][10][11][30]

claims.claim: Bimax or a single-jaw operation can fix a recessed jaw, and the result is often better than a jaw-jut test suggests.
Jaw surgery carries serious risks that are underreported, including permanent numbness.
Jaw surgery can improve function but disappoint cosmetically.
Jaw surgery is the way to get a 'chad' jaw and masculinise the face.
Getting insurance to cover jaw surgery depends on proving a functional problem.
Jaw surgery is a late-teen fix for people whose recession will not improve with growth.
People seeking jaw surgery are sometimes affected by body dysmorphic disorder.

timeline.event: Simon P. Hullihen publishes one of the first known orthognathic cases.[1]
Hugo Obwegeser is born; he later trains in Graz and becomes a leading figure in orthognathic surgery.[6]
Osteotomies of the jaws are developed for malocclusion and prognathism.[1]
The sagittal split and modern Le Fort I osteotomy are developed, with Obwegeser as a central figure.[2][6]
Obwegeser presents his techniques to North American surgeons at Walter Reed in Washington, D.C.[6]
Rigid titanium plate fixation reduces the need for long jaw immobilisation.[2]
A review of 655 patients reports the incidence of complications after orthognathic surgery.[25]
Raffaini introduces lower-jaw surgery under local anaesthesia with sedation, shortening hospital stay.[1]
An updated hierarchy of stability for orthognathic procedures with rigid fixation is published.[16]
A prospective multicentre study evaluates computer-aided surgical simulation accuracy.[17]
A systematic review estimates body dysmorphic disorder prevalence in orthognathic surgery settings at 11.2 percent.[27]
GQ reports growing demand among men for jaw surgery for a more masculine jawline.[12]
